thread.title: Apple: Don't Panic Below $150 - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Stone Fox Capital
title: Apple: Don't Panic Below $150 - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Despite all signs that the market already was bearish on Apple ( AAPL ), the company managed to disappoint investors even further. What my previous research saw as "Holiday Gifts" has turned into a situation where the Grinch has stolen the gifts. A lot of panic exists on what happens with China and whether iPhone average selling prices (ASPs) are too high, but the stock price is far too compelling here with the stock down nearly 40% and lots of positive signs still intermingled in the updated guidance .
Image Source: Apple website
China Problem The company spent the majority of the press release about cutting FQ1 numbers discussing the problems with emerging markets and particularly Greater China. The combination of the trade war and the gaming censorship in China likely contributed to the excessive weakness in their third largest market behind the Americas and Europe.
Based on data from last year, Apple had total FQ1 sales of $88.3 billion and Greater China sales of $18.0 billion. For sales to dip roughly $4.3 billion to $84 this FQ1, one has to assume a roughly 24% cut to Greater China sales to below $14 billion.
Source: Apple FQ1'18 summary data
Apple said this in the press release specifically about the Greater China revenue shortfall:
In fact, most of our revenue shortfall to our guidance, and over 100 percent of our year-over-year worldwide revenue decline occurred in Greater China across iPhone, Mac and iPad.
So this statement doesn't really solve how much of the cut from the original guidance was due to Greater China. Remember that Apple had recently guided to FQ1'19 revenues of $89 billion to $93 billion so at the mid point this updated guidance is a $7 billion cut. Assuming the cut in Greater China revenues was at least $5 billion of the guidance cut, other emerging market areas like Rest of Asia Pacific saw some big hits to expectations.
In our opinion, this is actually the silver lining in the guidance cut. A lot of the China issues can be played off as nationalism related to the trading wars and partially a by product of the Communist government not approving new online video games for most of 2018. The lack of new game approvals likely contributed to consumers not needing the latest iPhones to play these mobile games. The new game approvals at the end of December could provide a tailwind in 2019.
These issues are solvable over the near term as the US and China are likely to agree to a trade deal as these weak numbers hurt both countries. Also, the Chinese government recently started approving new mobile games. The end result will be a focus shift by the market to the sectors that are still strong:
Services - up 28% to $10.8 billion Wearables - up 50% YoY. Price Point Problem The clear indication before Apple came out with the guidance cut was that the company was having a problem with iPhone price points. Apple has the following iPhone trade-in deal on their website:
Source: Apple website
The deal allows consumers to grab a new iPhone at a reduced rate by trading in their used iPhones. The example above shows that an iPhone 8+ offers a $350 discount on a new X model.
Trade-in deals aren't new, but Apple got aggressive on the deals recently. The company needs these pre-owned phones to offer a discounted phone to emerging market consumers where a $1,000-plus phone isn't affordable for the masses.
The issue has propped up over the last few years as Apple has pushed the ASP from the $600 level in 2014 to recently reach close to $800 in the last quarter .
The ASP hike in the U.S. and Europe made sense to capture the high-end users shifting to holding smartphones for an extended period. The prime example is a premium phone going from $650 to $1,000 amounts to the same monthly price, if the user went from keeping smartphones for two years to three years.
Buyback To The Rescue The stock weakness brings an opportunity for a company with a net cash position of $130 billion ending December. Considering Apple ended the September quarter with $123 billion in cash, the company added about $7 billion to the net cash position during the last quarter.
Source: Apple return of capital history
A good question is what Apple did with cash during the quarter. Assuming the company generated about $25.5 billion in free cash flow like last year with slightly higher operating cash flows ($28.3 billion last FQ1) and capital expenditures ($2.8 billion last FQ1), the company returned about $18.5 billion to shareholders in the quarter. With quarterly dividends of $3.5 billion, share repurchases were around $15 billion.
The company placed the average share count for the quarter at 4.77 billion, down from 5.16 billion last year. The share count is down about 8% for the year and about 1.6% from the 4.85 billion shares last quarter.
The good news is that Apple pulled back from aggressive share buybacks during the quarter after having spent more than $20 billion per quarter in the prior three quarters of CY18. With the plan to become net-cash neutral, the tech giant remains in a strong position to repurchase up to 20% of the outstanding shares with the market cap down to $675 billion. This estimate doesn't even factor in a company generating $50 billion-plus in annual free cash flows depending on how these updated numbers impact cash flows going forward.
Investors need to keep these below EPS estimates in mind when considering that a lot of the shortfall could return once the China and emerging market problems are resolved. Upside to these numbers could actually occur as Apple is able to reduce the share count by an additional 5 percentage points with the $130 billion in net cash from when the stock had a market cap of $1 trillion.
AAPL EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts
The $14+ EPS estimate for FY20 could have 5% upside based on additional share repurchases. The numbers likely didn't even fully forecast the company reducing the share counts as expected, providing additional upside to estimates.
Naturally, the risk is that Apple doesn't recapture these lost sales in Greater China. In that scenario, the updated FY19 EPS estimates closer to $12 now still offer considerable value considering the company has $27 per share in cash.
At $142, Apple is back to trading below an EV of 10x EPS estimates. The company has downside protection in the event that business doesn't improve and substantial upside potential if Greater China revenues return.
Takeaway The key investor takeaway is that Apple made a strong case that the weakness is related to the trade wars and other China specific issues considering that diverse countries like the United States, Italy, Korea, Mexico and Vietnam saw record revenues. The tech giant likely needs to resolve a potential mounting iPhone price point issue, but the surging services and wearables revenues suggests the company can eventually overcome iPhone issues either way.
The stock is too cheap with or without a rebound in Greater China revenues. Based on my expectations that Apple has the potential to exceed original FY20 EPS estimates due in part to large stock buybacks, the stock has the potential to return to all-time highs in due course.
The market has extrapolated too far on some market weakness. Investors need to avoid the temptation to panic below $150 and remain in Apple for the long term.
